p: And now going into- back to MyCity, um, contracts, I wanna ask a little bit about, and I know my colleagues asked about like how many contracts are currently registered for work related to MyCity and we heard 117 was the number we heard. What is the total dollar value of these contracts?
I will defer to DC Choi.
Um, so total dollar value of those contracts is $135 million.
$135 million and do you know the typical duration of a contract for MyCity?
So every contract, um, may have a different duration because of the scope of work. Um, they can range from a few months to a year depending on what they're building.

Okay, can you break down a little bit for us, give us some clarity on this side, on the procurement method for the contracts? For

example, how many were delivery order as part of a master service agreement, and were any non-bid emergency contracts, no-bid emergency contracts?
Right. Um, so we always use the best procurement method, um, for the scope of work that we need. Um, I mentioned there's 117 contracts.
Mhm.
Um, 26 of them are direct orders, which is what I think you mean, um, leveraging, um, these reseller contracts.
26, yeah. All the other ones are MWBE, um, solicitations, so they were all competitive— competitively bid solicitations.

Um, there are several capital projects related to MyCity portal explicitly centered around the subject matter experts, meaning consultants. How many capital projects related to MyCity currently fund third-party vendors?

Yeah. So, um, our understanding, uh, my understanding of that question is any, um, subject matter experts that were attached to the contracts that I mentioned. Um, there are only 2, um, capital projects and there are consultants, um, supporting

multiple programs under MyCity. So child care application, the business services, um, so I can definitely give you more information if you—
Okay.
Have further questions.

Okay, um, I wanna, um, move on to the Office of Algorithmic Accountability. In November 2025, right here in her unlimited wisdom, um, former Chair Gutiérrez, uh, passed a law that would create the office, uh, uh, the GAARD Act, which among other things created the independent Office of Algorithmic Data Accountability within OTI. This office is charged with auditing, monitoring, and regulating agency AI tools, as well as investigating public complaints. To date, how much money has OTI allocated for the creation of the office?

Yeah, um, thanks for the question. Yes, uh, we have done work and planning, and we are standing up what needs to be stood up, I think, by June. Um, so that is all a work in progress in terms of the actual monies, uh, executed against it, I will once again defer to DC Choi.

Yeah, um, so we are, uh, reviewing the scope needed to accomplish the local law. We're

working with OMB. We're trying to evaluate our existing resources to see if we can fulfill that. Um, we have had conversations with City Hall leadership about appointing the director of the office, so we hope to accomplish that by -by June.
Do we have an estimate, um, for how much it will cost for creating the office?
We are, we are continuing to assess what our internal, um, priorities are and, um, the needs to accomplish the goals of the local law. So we are in discussions.
Okay, and I'm assuming that the staffing level and all of that is also up for discussion?
Correct.
Okay.
And yeah, just to build on that, I think the idea is for us to actually really think about what's required and what the outcomes we are shooting for and that will define how we need to staff it.

Great, okay. Did that. Okay. I wanna ask about citywide contracts. OTI

holds a number of citywide contracts for technology-related services provided to all city agencies. For example, the Microsoft software suite and telecommunication services. How many citywide contracts does OTI hold and for what services exactly?

Thank you for that question. Yeah, it's, that's one of the things that I have learned, uh, is just how much we are supporting the other agencies by providing these master contracts that they can, uh, pull from. So it's really great that we have created these unified vehicles. Um, in terms of which ones exist and how much they are spending on, I will defer to D.C. Pemberton.
Thank you, CTO. So total, as far as, uh, OTI total contracts, we have approximately 224.
Can you say it again?

224 contracts. And some of these contracts, we go to work with agencies to create like enterprise license agreements. So it evolves into something where agencies had contracts by themselves. We work with Microsoft as a vendor. We bring in their licenses together, we save money

far as, you know, increase volume and leveraging, and we create these multi-year contracts so the current agencies can use it and new agencies who have that need could actually piggyback as well.
Okay, um, do you have, um, how does OTI negotiate these contracts?

Well, the first starts from, uh, most of the time, a lot of vendors understand that the cities have savings needs. They come to us, they actually put together some proof of concept. From that concept, we validate with each agency's CIO, CFOs, and then we come back to that, um, that agency, um, that vendor to actually negotiate. In addition to negotiating, we send out for, um, private benchmarking to validate national pricing. And after we finish our proposal, submit to OMB, and they also do QC on exactly the benefits of entering those agreements.
Okay. Um, does— do contracts under OTI have subcontracting limits? What transparency— what is the transparency for examining subcontractors within the contracts?
At OTI, we validate that all our contracts have to be going through MWBE programs first.
Mhm.
When they don't go through MWBE programs, we make sure that there's still that 30% subcontracting from that, that prime should be—
That's the limit.
Right?
Okay. Okay, um, that, that tracks. Okay and then does OTI hold any no-bid emergency contracts?
No, we do not hold any no-bid emergency contracts.
Do you believe that change— that any changes need to be made to the process for securing citywide contracts?
I'll let you go first.

I, I think as we enter in, um, this savings, uh, initiative, it is widening that we, we should move to, to proactively look and see wherever, wherever there's redundancy in for the IT world so that we do get that leverage and power that we need. And that's definitely something any agency

should come to us, vice versa, we go to them to, to, to get that leverage and power.

Yeah and I would just similarly, I do think we have to explore, um, how the interaction between OTI and agencies work now. Are there more opportunities we could do it? And I think, you know, some of the ones that are obvious are forward-facing, right? Like Microsoft but there is also a lot of, uh, back— like, um, behind the scenes, um, uh, contracts. And so I think the right approach is understanding what other agencies need, what they're using, and are there economies of scale that we could get if we brought it into one? But also we wanna allow the agencies to be as nimble as they need to be, right? We don't want to put blockers into place for them to get the work done. So that's that balance that we have to do.

Great. Thank you for answering those questions. I'm gonna ask about LinkNYC and then we'll pass it to Council Member Gutiérrez. Um, launched in 2015, LinkNYC aims to replace public pay phones with kiosks that offer free calling, mobile device charging, access to 911 and 311.

LinkNYC also began installing 5G towers across the city. The program operates on a franchise agreement. The contract company pays the city for the use of sidewalk space and operates the kiosk, generating their profit from advertising revenue. In Fiscal 2019, CityBridge, the company that to this day operates LinkNYC kiosk, only paid $2.6 million of the $32.3 million owed to the city under the terms of the agreement. Under the terms of the franchise agreement, how much did CityBridge owe the city in Fiscal '25, and how much did they pay?
Sorry, I didn't hear that. Under— yeah, I didn't hear that last part.
How much did CityBridge— does CityBridge owe the city in Fiscal '25, and how much did they pay?
Got it. Uh, I am going to defer to, uh, DC Pemberton for that answer.
Currently, CityBridge is, is up to date, um, with their payments.
Mhm.
And, um, I'll get you that number in a second.
For Fiscal '25 and '26 so far?
Yeah, yes. Hold on a second. Sorry. So CityBridge, um, has paid the city out of the $87.5 million that's owed um, in the overall proposal, they have, uh, paid $48.4 million to the city.
Okay. Um, what is OTI's projection that they will owe in the out years?
Well, roughly right now, they, they owe— they're less than 50% there, so - the difference is already in the grid. We could send you the— those, uh, contracts.
That would be great.
I'm sorry. Can I ask, is there a cons— I don't know if I'm supposed to do this, but is there a concern about their payments?
Yeah, we just wanna make sure that we are tracking and that we know how much of the payment has been made just for—
Okay, thanks.

Um, and then do we know how often CityBridge makes the payment to the city? Um, has made payments to the city on time since

fiscal 2019? So just to track how much they've paid and if they're paying on time.
We meet quarterly with CityBridge, and we have no problems with them paying on time.
Okay.
Otherwise we would have, um, instituted penalties.

Okay, great. Thank you for clarifying. I'll pass it to Council Member Gutiérrez. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Chair. Um, I just had one more question about, um, the MyCity app. My apologies. Oh no, about Big Apple Connect. It's a lot. It's a lot. Um, so about Big Apple Connect, I think, um, you know, I think, I think the, the questions were great and I, I do believe that there, there's like an immense service there and, um, at least for the folks in my community that are registered, that do have the service, I think for the most part they're very happy with it and it's great to be able to connect. I was very happy, uh, later in, in the last term to hear that OTI had put together this digital equity roadmap

because those were a lot of my questions in the beginning about connecting public housing residents, uh, to NYCHA and really like missing an opportunity to connect them with, you know, the tools to use that. So, um, I, I'm, I'm encouraged by that. I just wanted to ask for the future of Big Apple Connect, because I know, I believe it's, it's funded, and I'm sorry if I missed that.

That's okay. Uh, we, this- in Fiscal '26, we signed a 3-year renewal. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Um, can you share a little bit more? Because this Council was a little bit taken aback by, there was an article that was released in the spring of last year that really said, um, that kind of pointed to Big Apple Connect and the, the access that PD had to use, um, you know, the, the bandwidth that was being, uh, secured for NYCHA, for NYCHA tenants for their own purpose of, you know, surveillance or whatever it is. Um, can you share if that is still, if that is still a practice, if that is specific to the contract in this new extension?

Uh, I will share what I believe is the answer, and somebody can correct me if I'm wrong. But, um, um, so the contract we have is with NYCHA to provide these Wi-Fi services and so who has access to them, uh, is anybody kind of through those, uh, those programs or connections through NYCHA. Uh, so, uh, so we all— our job is to provide the Wi-Fi. And so, yeah, I can't really speak to— COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: So PD- PD does not have a contract with OTI? To be able to tap into the service? It's just

So the nature of the Big Apple Connect agreement is that there is the ability for any city agency to use that bulk pricing for the purposes of connecting. So yes, there is a, a, you know, an amount that, uh, that NYPD pays us with respect to that under that contract. However, the relationship between NYCHA and NYPD is an existing one. So to the extent that NYCHA decides to provide this, um, uh, access to NYPD, that's between them. And there's an MOU with respect to that, from my understanding. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: There's an MOU and are you all not privy to how they're used? Like, ah, are

you— because it's an MOU between NYCHA and PD, are you all not just not involved in that?

That is correct. We're not involved in that and it's like every city agency just asks for the widgets. We don't know how the widgets are used. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Yeah. Do you all have any reason to be concerned about, uh, data privacy and the way that PD is potentially using Big Apple Connect for, like, biometric, um, scanning or any— of public housing residents? Is there any reason for you all to believe as an agency under this Administration that there might be some loopholes here that PD is potentially using, um, specifically in public housing.

That would be— COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: I'm surprised that PD needs access to internet is what I'm, I'm surprised, especially in NYCHA. They, uh, are a multimillion-dollar agency and I'm just surprised that they need to— and they, they've been in public housing, like you said, this relationship is pre-existing in the Big Apple Connect.

So I'm just- I don't - I'm very concerned with, um, the news last year um, that they have this MOU with NYCHA specific to, like, being able to connect to the, the, the bandwidth, if I'm using that, um, correctly. And I think that there is, like, reasonable fear that people have about how they're connecting. Um, do they have access to people's, like, personal, uh, you know, connection in, in their residences? I think that— you're looking at me with a funny face. Are you following what I'm saying, or—

No, no, I'm following what you're saying, but um, unfortunately we can't answer for NYPD, so I'm trying to determine if there's— COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: I'm not— yeah, totally and I'm not asking for PD perspective. I'm asking for you all as an agency that's providing the service, if you have concerns, if you have data pri— if you have privacy concerns, if you have the fact that like they are specifically— this is a completely new MOU that PD went into agreement with, with NYCHA, separate from everything else they already do in public housing to be able to connect? Do you all have that concern?

So, uh, from a technological perspective, I'll answer the best that I can, which is we're providing the connectivity, um, from a data security and privacy perspective, which is also very important to us. Um, providing connectivity should not, um, allow anybody to like watch other people's bits, right? So if you and I are on the same, uh, Wi-Fi or, you know, like I should not be able to— if, if data is encrypted, uh, end-to-end, right? What you're doing, I can't see. And so what we have provided is the connectivity. But, um, independent of the connectivity, uh, all of the agencies have to, uh, adhere to, uh, privacy and security requirements, right, that we're working— that we are— that we put out, the guidance that we put out. So kind of as two separate things, uh, connectivity-wise, technologically, we're not facilitating— I don't wanna use the word spying, but we're not, right? They can't watch your bits. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Uh, and I mean, that's what, that's what I wanna hear.

Yeah. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: I don't, it's not clear if that is clear to PD and it's certainly not

clear to NYCHA residents who brought it to our attention.

I mean, I believe, I, I believe this did come up during the previous hearing and PD did explain their policies. So, um, I believe some of that information is there in terms of exactly when and how they access. Like, for instance, based purely on my own recollection, they only access when there is an incident and for particular periods of time, for instance. So there are like standards in place because they do have policies. I just don't know the specifics of those policies. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: And then as part of the extension, the 1-year extension, it's based— this, this exists. There's no— there was no change, um, on your part.

No and again, I, I just, I wanna distinguish, and I'm pretty sure I'm right technologically, but we can get back to you to confirm, but PD cannot see residents' bits because they're on the same Wi-Fi. PD can see their own bits. Right, which is, I think, a distinction.

COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Okay and I mean, I think there was—
I just wanted to add that it's common areas. It's common area Wi-Fi. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Yeah.
So it's, it's my understanding that's not in the apartments. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Well, I think, I think up until that hearing we were not— I think it was unclear, uh, to folks.

Gotcha. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: And I think that there were a significant amount of NYCHA residents that came to testify where they felt like they were already being surveilled by PD on night— on their NYCHA campus. And so really had strong feelings about how the city was allowing them to have like hyper-connectivity in hallways and in lobbies, uh, to be able to like what they felt was like additional, like layered surveillance. Um, okay. I mean, I would love to continue this, this conversation. It 100% is a conversation with PD as well. Um, sorry, my last question is just about the digital equity roadmap that I mentioned at the

top. Um, I think it was a good road— roadmap. I think it referenced actually a lot of what— a lot of the work that the City Council had already been doing. And I think I would love to hear more about how you all think the roadmap will be a part of the internet master plan. What kind of the funding I will say from what I remember, and I could be wrong, was not, was not, maybe not all there was not into the out years. And so would love to hear kind of what the advocacy plan is there. Um, and if there's any, if there's any, like, if there's any feedback, um, I know that there was specific partnerships with, you know, NYCHA senior centers, um, with some of the hubs, the citywide hubs, and I'm using the wrong verbiage, and no disrespect, I'm so sorry, but I would just love to hear more about how you guys are thinking about funding for meeting some of those goals in the out years. And that's it. Thank you.
Absolutely. I would ask, uh, for Joe and Sam to switch things. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: And Joe, thank you so much for being here. I have nothing for you, but good to see you.

Uh, so yes, um, Associate Commissioner Wright has invested a lot of time in thinking in terms of coming up with, uh, a, uh, thoughtful broadband adoption plan, and it includes a bunch of different pieces, uh, which she can go over.

Thank you, CTO, and thank you, Gutiérrez, for this question. Um, as I mentioned, we have been investing a lot of time and energy into rolling out the initiatives that were outlined in the Digital Equity Roadmap. Um, we are also coming up on the 1-year anniversary of the, uh, release of that report. Um, as you mentioned, there were, uh, capital investments outlined in that report, $2.4 million. Um, as you mentioned, uh, a portion of that was going to NYC Aging to replace, um, outdated technology in the older adult centers, uh, purchasing a new, uh, digital van for NYCHA, um, as well as updating technology in NYPL TechConnect branches. Um, most of that work is, uh, nearing completion. Um, one of the other key priorities that was outlined in the Digital Equity Roadmap was the creation of the Chief Digital Equity Officer and creation of a Digital Equity Manager role, uh, to

spearhead this work. Um, as I mentioned earlier, they were, uh, welcomed to OTI, uh, this past summer, uh, and we have been really hunkered down thinking about these issues, mapping out the plan, uh, for OTI and the city going forward. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Chair.

Thank you. I wanted to ask about DOE Chromebook maintenance and connectivity new need. The Preliminary Plan includes $36.5 million of city funding in Fiscal ‘26 only for the LTE connection services associated with 350,000 new Chromebooks distributed by the public school— uh, distributed to public school students. Uh, why is that— why was additional funding required, and how was the amount determined?
Thank you for the question. I will defer to, uh, DC Choi.

Hmm, thank you, CTO. Um, so this initiative, the DOE Chromebooks, is actually part of a larger digital equity, um, um, purpose and objective. We wanted to make sure all of public schools, uh, students had access to digital devices, especially at home.

So the- the initiative that was rolled out last year was connected to a larger contract with T-Mobile that the city negotiated. So as part of that T-Mobile contract, DOE Chromebook devices, um, was, um, uh, laid out in terms of the cost of, um, connectivity for up to a million devices.
Okay and does, um, how long does OTI plan to keep the Chromebooks LTE connected, and how long is the contract for?

Right. Um, for the length of the contract, I'll defer to, um, D.C. Pemberton. Um, the Chromebooks, uh, the 350,000, the rollout of it completed in February of this year. So our hope is to continue, um, the connectivity through this Fiscal Year for the school, um, and then as long as we have, um, funding available to continue that, um, access for the students at home. So as long as there's resources to do so. If the connectivity is um, for some reason or another cut, are the Chromebooks then, um, not useful?

So there's connectivity at schools, um, where, where the Chromebooks are also being used. And then at home, um, we talked about the Big Apple Connect program. Um, again, our, um, priority here

is to make sure all the students are connected. So we hope to continue funding this program.
Great.
Right? Connectivity— if there's Wi-Fi, they're connected. So add a link, uh, at NYC Link, for example.

Okay, okay. Um, more on that, but we— I know we have the education hearing on Monday, so we'll ask some questions there. Um, but how was T-Mobile chosen as the provider, and what is the rate paid to them?
DC Pemberton.

Thank you, CTO. T-Mobile, uh, is a carrier that we had already in, in our procurement, um, uh, I guess, um, solicitations. We had T-Mobile, Verizon, and AT&T. So what we do sometimes is engage in competitive pricing and it was some— something similar to that, just to say who has the best price. And we was able to look at price and quality to make that award.
And how much was the total value?
The total value of, of that contract, um, for T-Mobile is $198 million for, for LTE services.
I'm sorry, $198 million is, is the total value of that contract for LTE services.
And for how long?
Right, right now it's for 4 years.
4 years.
And just for clarity, is that contract just for the Chromebooks LTE?
The contract has Chromebooks LTE plus the, uh, wireless, um, cost included.

Got it, okay, got it. Thank you for going into that. I wanna ask about asylum seeker adjustments. The Preliminary Plan includes $20.8 million reduction in Fiscal Year '26 related to asylum seeker response efforts. What programs or services does this reduction relate to and why is the reduction required and how was the amount determined? LISA GELOBTER; Thank you for that question. Uh, I am also just learning about some of this stuff and

getting up to speed, so I would like to defer to— oh, to, uh, DC Pemberton.
Thank you CTL. So, so the asylum seeker, um, reduction is due to the fact that when the original budget was, um, um, developed, we had a contingency for buildouts of more, um, shelters.
Mhm.
But since it's been ramped, ramping down, we worked with OMB to reduce that budget.

Makes sense and is OCI's Host Technology System for asylum seeker response efforts still operational? Are there plans for it to be sunset, or does the Administration intend to maintain its current functionality?
We, we're currently working with, um, um, the asylum seeker program with City Hall and, and we'll, we'll be reevaluating our budget in the next, um, cycle exec plan.
And then in parallel, right, what, what are the needs still?

Mhm. Yeah, that makes sense. Um, okay, we've been joined by Council Member

Brewer and she has questions, but I'm gonna ask my last round of questions and I'll pass to her. Um, there's funding that's reflected in the budget for several Adams Administration initiatives. Um, the plan does not include funding that can be clearly identified for several initiatives created under Adams Administration. For example, the New York City Smart City Testbed program, the New York City Blockchain initiatives, and the New York City— well, we already asked about the digital roadmap. Can you verify if there's any budgeted expenses or capital funding for these programs? If so, how much in each— in which Fiscal Years? And can you work with our Finance Staff to clarify a way they can find this funding in the agency's budget. We kind of had a hard time tracking it.

Yeah. Um, before we jump in, I, I just, I also am coming from a point of view, that just because something was invented in the previous Administration does not make it inherently bad. So as we're gonna do with everything else, we're gonna actually figure out what makes sense for us, how we wanna move forward. So yeah. And I will hand off to— DC Choi.
Thank you, CTO. So for the, uh, New York City Smart City Testbed and the New York City Blockchain Initiatives, um, there are no budgeted expense or capital funding needs.
Say it again, sorry.
There, there's no funding for either of those programs.
Okay. Um, okay. And so I guess you're reevaluating if these programs will continue, which we, um, which we know. And is there a timeline for the evaluation overall?
At the moment, no. I, 2 weeks in, but yes, I have grand visions.
Thank you, thank you so much. Uh, Council Member Brewer?
Ah, welcome, Commissioner. I've known her since she's born, so this is very exciting.
I've heard you used to babysit me.
Very exciting. Congratulations. Well, the whole— your whole environment is very, very pleased.
Thank you.

Me too. So, um, two things. One is just on the big picture. I read your testimony. This is my third hearing, different topic, so I'm sorry I wasn't here earlier, but I did read your testimony. My question is, the work that you did on the education, uh, at the federal level, figuring out, you know, how people can better analyze when they go into college and so on, what would be some example of something here they could use that kind of fabulous, uh, new viewing? Because unfortunately, in this city, there's just, I think, a lot of projects that could use that rethink. And I'm just wondering, that's more like a bigger picture than some of these other questions, but what you did on that level for the applicants to college was phenomenal.

Thank you, I appreciate it. And most importantly, uh, that project was credited with improving college graduation rates in the U.S., which is really the thing that matters. So, um, yeah, and I think that that is the- the exact brand of, uh, of approach that we— that I think we're gonna try to bring to, um, to New York City government as well.

Um, two things in particular that made that program successful, uh, one is rather than just do the same old thing or the status quo or take explicit direction. So I actually was told by the President of the United States what to do and I went, thank you for your advice and your input. And then really backed up and said, well, what is the problem we're trying to solve? And so we really— so rather than being boxed in on what exists, we really want to be able to step back and take initiative. And again, that means going out and talk- getting out of the building and talking to users and talking to agencies and understanding and really understanding the needs. And again, the problem trying to solve, not this is how, this is how it's always done. So that's one big part of it that, made, I think, a huge difference. The second part of it was open data. Um, so-
That's my bill. That's the one I passed.
Don't you forget it.
Yeah, exactly. I do not let anybody forget it.
It was great. Um, but it is— but that's—
It needs updating, though.

Okay, but that's the thing that makes the difference, right? So the answer is— the password for our project was "Set the Data Free," right? The idea is the government can do- has a limited amount of resources, has a very specific perspective. If the data is open and accessible, like, listen to the crowds, right? Different people with different perspectives can extract information, make, uh, uh, make suggestions based on that. So yeah, open data is critical.

So that's— I should know this, but usually it comes in the Office of Operations, but also you all work together. It's like a collaborative effort, if it needs improving as an open data platform, correct? Or is it just operations?
Um, I thought that, um, it was ours, right?
